body:
• India has lavished money on its startups — the Fund of Funds mobilised Rs 25,500+ crore into 1,370+ startups, with a Rs 1 lakh crore RDI Fund behind it — but government buying hasn't followed: startups won just over Rs 19,000 crore of Rs 5.03 lakh crore in Government e-Marketplace purchases in FY26, under 4%.
  • "India changed the rules of entry. It did not change the incentives of the buyer." Exemptions from deposits and relaxed turnover norms (GFR Rules 170/173) help startups apply — but no ministry has a target to buy from them.
  • The contrast is the MSE procurement mandate: a 25% floor plus reporting produced 43.58% procurement from small enterprises. Startups, YourStory argues, are "the only priority category in Indian public procurement that received relief on the entry side and nothing at all on the buyer side."
  • Defence and space prove the model works: iDEX's buy-without-re-tendering rule, a Rs 511 crore SSLV tech transfer to HAL, and Skyroot's Vikram-1 reaching orbit in July 2026 show what happens when the state becomes a customer, not just an investor.

India funds its startups generously. It just won't buy from them. That is the thesis of a new YourStory analysis, backed by numbers showing a decade of Startup India policy built a formidable funding machine — while leaving the buying side almost untouched.

The figures are stark. In FY26, the Government e-Marketplace (GeM) processed Rs 5.03 lakh crore in purchases. Startups received just over Rs 19,000 crore — under 4% — against Rs 2.36 lakh crore (47.1%) for small enterprises. Fewer than one in five recognised startups is even registered as a government seller; a Standing Committee on Commerce found only 10% had transacted on GeM at all across eight financial years, worth Rs 14,000 crore in total.

All entry, no incentive

Since 2016, Startup India has rolled out tax incentives, seed funding and incubators; GFR Rules 170 and 173 exempt recognised startups from deposits and allow relaxed turnover and experience requirements; GeM's Startup Runway (launched November 2019) lists innovative products under 14 subsectors with minimal specs.

But none of it tells a buyer to buy. "MSEs have a procurement mandate. Startups have exemptions," YourStory writes. "One tells the buyer: you must buy. The other tells the startup: you may apply." Every ministry, department and central PSU must source at least 25% of procurement from micro and small enterprises — a floor that produced 43.58% in 2024-25. Startups got the red carpet at the door and silence at the counter.

"A grant can help a startup build a prototype. Only a customer can help it build a company."

— YourStory

Why money outruns orders

The blockage is bureaucratic incentives: a grant is administratively safe; a purchase order to a three-year-old company invites audit queries. Ministries became investors rather than customers — "the proliferation of PSU startup funds is not a solution to procurement rigidity. It is a symptom of it." Punishing contract terms compound the pain: ONGC's standard liquidated damages of 0.5% a week up to 10% mean "the biggest order in a young company's history" can become "the order that kills it."

Where buying worked: defence and space

The exceptions prove the rule. Defence's iDEX, launched in 2018, was folded into the Defence Acquisition Procedure 2020, allowing purchase of iDEX-developed products without re-tendering, with grants up to Rs 25 crore and assured five-plus-five-year orders. In space, the Rs 511 crore SSLV technology transfer to HAL, Skyroot's Vikram-1 reaching orbit in July 2026 — India's first privately developed orbital rocket — and a Defence Department order for 31 satellites from private firms show a pipeline that buys what it funds. IN-SPACe chairman Pawan Goenka has put it bluntly: "the government has to be an anchor customer."

States are experimenting

Several states are improvising. Kerala allows direct startup purchases without tender up to Rs 50 lakh — 264 work orders worth Rs 28.05 crore. Rajasthan's iStart and e-Bazaar channelled Rs 22+ crore in work orders; Telangana offers a 15% price preference; Maharashtra earmarks 0.5% of departmental budgets for innovation.

The ask: a 1% Purchase Order Mission

YourStory's proposed fix costs no new money: a "1% Purchase Order Mission" — 1% of central procurement earmarked for DPIIT-recognised startups — roughly Rs 5,000 crore a year — plus pilot-to-order conversion without re-tendering, startup-specific contract terms, and quarterly ministry-wise public reporting. The US offers a template in the SBIR program's Phase III, where agencies may award sole-source contracts with no cap: "India built the qualifying round twenty times over. Outside defence, it never built the prize."

With the DPIIT Deep Tech category, Railways' Rail Tech Policy 2026 and NITI Aayog's civilian-iDEX discussion paper all live, "the task is migration rather than invention." The money is flowing. What's missing is a customer.
diaspora_angle: Diaspora founders and Indian-origin deep-tech investors eyeing India as a first customer face exactly this friction: the state funds but won't buy — access to customers, not capital, is the binding constraint.
headline: India Funds Its Startups Lavishly. So Why Won't It Buy From Them?
subheadline: Startups won under 4% of Rs 5.03 lakh crore in government marketplace purchases last year despite a decade of funding schemes. The problem, a new analysis argues, isn't capital — it's that no one has to buy.
